prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable optical clocks of unprecedented stability and accuracy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read the full first round, I find the scientific core of the case unaffected by the objections. The invention is the magic-wavelength lattice: it cancels the differential light shift of the clock transition, and Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil broadening. This lets a very large number of neutral atoms be interrogated on a narrow optical line, so one gets ensemble stability and single-system accuracy at once. That is a different mechanism from the comb, which is a readout tool for optical frequencies (2005), and from the control of single trapped ions (2012). Independent laboratories now run and compare such clocks near 1e-18, and the same clocks are used for millimetre-scale relativistic redshift, constraints on varying constants and a coming redefinition of the second. The credit divides naturally between Katori for the concept and first realisation, and Ye for taking stability, coherence and accuracy to the extreme regime. No third name is needed. The chair asks whether the redefinition should count as maturity evidence. I say it is a consequence of settled physics and not a reason to give or withhold the prize, so I would keep it out of the citation. The citation should name the lattice clock and its magic-wavelength trapping, not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy generally, which answers the distinctness question for those who doubt it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes: a sceptic may read the lattice clock as an extraordinary refinement of a recognised lineage. I weigh this less because the citation can state the distinct mechanism explicitly, but I cannot make it vanish. Second, the credit is not complete. Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates and other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups, and the collective-effect and laser-coherence work in Ye's group, sit outside two names, and the division between concept and performance is partly intertwined. I recall the early priority sequence from general knowledge and cannot verify it from the committee files, which the chair rightly asks us to do. Third, a committee could prefer to wait until the SI redefinition is concluded. I think that is a timing preference and not a scientific argument.

responses.point: Danielsson moved the lattice clock to first place and asks that the citation name the lattice-clock architecture, not precision spectroscopy in general, and keep the SI redefinition out of the citation. Danielsson also says that Ludlow and Lemonde belong to the normal long tail of a prize.
responses.response: I agree on both points of wording, and the citation I propose is written that way: it names the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping and does not mention the redefinition. I accept the long-tail argument for Ludlow and Lemonde only in part. The tail is acceptable when the two credited names are the originators, and here the intertwining of Katori's concept with Ye's early demonstrations is the thing I cannot verify from the files. I therefore do not claim that the two names are beyond challenge, only that no evidence we hold supports a third. I also note that Danielsson would turn to twistronics if the committee wanted a condensed-matter prize. I still regard that as a prize for a later year, because its interpretation is moving.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B007 as the sole part and says that if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is judged indispensable, the three-name limit cannot give a fair attribution. Olsson also lists the lattice clock as an alternative and admits that Ludlow and Lemonde might weigh more on closer inspection.
responses.response: I take your own test seriously: a prediction confirmed by a specific measurement is what I trust as an experimentalist, and the lattice clock meets it through agreement between independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level. On B007 I find the chair's question decisive for me. As far as I can judge from the exchange, nobody in round 1 argued that the HgTe experiment would have been proposed without the BHZ work, and your caution about Zhang's death means that no three-name list can repair the omission. Reworded citation text can state the Z2 mechanism and so answer the 2016 overlap, but wording cannot fix a missing person. That is why B007 stays my first alternative and not my lead. If the committee were to find that the BHZ proposal was not indispensable, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Johansson accepts B056 and adds Hosono (B037) as a second part for iron-based high-temperature superconductivity, using exactly three names, and argues that the open pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap and not a gap in the discovery.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of a second part with a single unambiguous discoverer, and I agree that the discovery of the iron-based superconductors is mature and well replicated. I do not support the pairing. You yourself say the two parts have almost nothing in common, and I do not find that a prize should be assembled from two unrelated achievements to fit a three-name limit. Hosono's support among colleagues is thin, and I have no evidence from the files that the rapid follow-on Tc-raising work by other groups was less decisive than the original discovery. The lattice clock needs no companion to be complete, and adding a part that attracts little support would dilute the strongest case on the shortlist. If the committee later wants a second part, I would first look at the achievements closest in field and maturity, rather than B037.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to the lattice clock and says the comb prize honoured an enabling technology, so a third name from other groups would not be supported by the evidence. Pearce also lists the pending redefinition as a possible weighting of the prize by metrology politics.
responses.response: I agree that widening to a third name is not supported by the evidence in the files, and I would keep the credit at two. I part from you on one nuance. You say you cannot verify priority independently and rely on recollection, and so do I and several others. That is a shared weakness: four of us supporting the clock recall the same history from general knowledge. I would therefore ask the committee, before the vote, not to lean on any claim of priority in the citation text. The citation can stand on the invention and development of the lattice clock, which is documented as distinct and as reproduced by independent laboratories, and not on who was first by weeks or months.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B007 and would keep the citation centred on the concept, accepting the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap as a regrettable unfairness. Eriksson also asks whether the lattice clock should take precedence on grounds of timeliness.
responses.response: I respect the scientific argument that Z2 classification changed how band structures are analysed, and I agree it is mature. But accepting a known credit gap as regrettable is a different judgement from mine, since the Nobel Prize is a statement about who made the discovery. Because the lattice clock has a clean pair, I prefer not to knowingly make that compromise when an alternative without it is available. Your own remark on timeliness is one I would not rely on: the redefinition of the second does not make the physics more or less ready. I would answer your question that the clock should take precedence because of settled physics, independent reproduction and clean attribution, not because of the calendar.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I judge it to be, with the citation naming magic-wavelength lattice trapping.

The exact priority sequence between Katori's concept and the first lattice-clock demonstrations, and the weight of Ye's group in the early work, which I recall from general knowledge and which the committee files do not document.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates or others should have been credited, and whether the committee would view a two-person prize as too narrow.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal was indispensable to the HgTe experiment; if not, B007 would move up for me.
Whether an unspoken preference to wait for the SI redefinition will affect others' votes.
statement.conflict_note: No disqualifying conflict. For transparency: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Hall belongs to the 2005 frequency-comb background of the clock field. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. As an atomic and laser physicist I am professionally close to the field. The chair asks about recusal: I see no specific trigger, I would accept the committee's judgement if it advised otherwise. My Lund colleagues named in my profile (Rippe, Walther, Kinos) and my Deep Light Vision and WACQT roles do not connect to any shortlisted name.
